Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for seeing Mrs. Clara Higgins, an 80-year-old retired bookkeeper, for your assessment of her persistent skin lesions, which she recalls first developing during her early childhood.

On physical examination, she demonstrates numerous tiny, firm, seed-like keratotic deposits scattered across the volar aspects of her hands and the weight-bearing surfaces of her feet. These minute lesions present clinically as discrete, heavily cornified raised papules that cause her mild tenderness when walking. A recent punch biopsy taken from her left heel demonstrated marked widening of the granular cell layer. Notably, no retention of nuclei was observed within the stratum corneum.

Other examined structures were completely unremarkable. Her teeth display standard contour and development, with no structural anomalies. Examination of her hair was entirely normal, showing preserved shaft architecture and standard texture. Furthermore, the nail plates across all digits were clear and intact, showing no ridging, thickening, or architectural dystrophy.

Mrs. Higgins takes only a daily calcium tablet and an over-the-counter multivitamin. Her cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were entirely normal, with unremarkable baseline vitals, and she has no family history of similar cutaneous changes. 

I would greatly appreciate your expert assessment regarding her case.

Warm regards,

Dr. Thomas Vance
